query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr has 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but its poor oxygen resistance limits practical high-temperature use. What single intervention could overcome this limitation without sacrificing the alloy’s useful mechanical performance? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention and mechanism, the predicted change relative to untreated cast HfNbTaTiZr, the relevant temperature, atmosphere, exposure time, and mechanical-loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Applying an ultrathin, dense, and well‐adhered anti-oxidation coating (e.g., an alumina film deposited via atomic layer deposition) on cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr will significantly improve its oxygen resistance during high-temperature exposure without degrading its intrinsic mechanical performance.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr in its as-cast state, exhibiting 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C (at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1), but with poor oxygen resistance.
generation.intervention: Deposit an ultrathin (e.g., 50–100 nm), uniform alumina (Al2O3) coating on the alloy surface via atomic layer deposition (ALD).
generation.conditions: High-temperature exposure in air (oxidizing atmosphere) at ~1000 °C for durations on the order of tens to hundreds of hours; mechanical tests performed at similar temperature and strain rate boundaries as in the baseline measurements.
generation.structural_mediator: The conformal Al2O3 coating acts as a physical oxygen barrier that prevents oxygen pickup and subsequent embrittlement along grain boundaries and surfaces.
generation.mechanism: By virtue of its high density and excellent chemical inertness, the ALD-deposited alumina layer impedes oxygen diffusion into the underlying refractory high-entropy alloy; this preserves the microstructural integrity and thus maintains the alloy's ductility and yield strength at high temperature.
generation.predicted_outcome: Treated samples will exhibit markedly improved oxidation resistance (i.e., lower oxygen uptake and reduced oxide scale formation) during prolonged high-temperature exposure while retaining similar tensile ductility at room temperature and yield strength at elevated temperatures compared to untreated samples.
generation.baseline: Untreated cast HfNbTaTiZr, which shows significant oxidation-related degradation under high-temperature air exposure.
generation.boundary: The intervention is expected to be effective provided that the coating remains adherent and intact under thermal cycling and mechanical loading; performance should be validated for exposures around 1000 °C in air and strain rates between 10−4–10−2 s−1.
generation.uncertainty: Uncertainties include the long-term adhesion and thermal stability of the ultrathin alumina coating under cyclic thermal and stress conditions, and potential spallation or microcracking that could eventually compromise the barrier effect.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of as-cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr specimens: one group receives the ALD-deposited alumina coating and the other remains uncoated (control). Expose both groups to a high-temperature oxidizing environment (1000 °C in air) for a fixed duration (e.g., 100 hours). After exposure, perform high-temperature tensile tests at strain rates of 10−4 to 10−2 s−1 and assess microstructural changes using cross-sectional microscopy and oxygen content measurements.
measurements: High-temperature yield strength and ductility from tensile tests
Oxide scale thickness and composition using SEM/TEM and EDS
Oxygen depth profiles (e.g., via SIMS) in the substrate after exposure
Adhesion integrity and possible spallation of the coating (e.g., via scratch testing)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the alumina-coated samples do not show a statistically significant reduction in oxygen uptake or if their mechanical properties (yield strength and ductility) deteriorate significantly compared to the control after high-temperature exposure, then the hypothesis that the ALD alumina coating effectively improves oxygen resistance without sacrificing mechanical performance is falsified.

In 2004, Professor Yeh and his group published the concept of high-entropy alloys (HEAs) []. He defined high-entropy alloys (HEAs) as having five or more major elements beneath 5–35 at.%, and minor elements below five at.%. In 2006, he also established four core effects of HEAs []: High-entropy, severe-lattices-distortion, sluggish-diffusion, and the cocktail effect. With the new concepts, scientists are able to develop and expand alloys without restrictions [,,,,]. Some HEAs have been found to have attractive properties on diffusion [], oxidation [], corrosion [], fatigue [], creep [], fracture toughness [], and elevated-temperature strength []. High-entropy superalloys (HESAs) [], eutectic HEAs (EHEAs) [], light-weight HEAs (LWHEAs) [], refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) [], etc. have been proposed and attract increased attention. In 2010, Senkov and Miracle first published RHEAs, MoNbTaW and MoNbTaVW [,]. These two alloys possess body-centered cubic (BCC) structure and have excellent elevated-temperature yield strength which is around 400 MPa at 1600 °C.
